source.text: The monk Yaun (late Goryeo), Self-Admonitions: the third part of the Admonitions for Beginners (Chobalsim Jagyeongmun)
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

j01.heading: Master, Listen to Me
j01.plain: Master within, listen to me. So many people have attained the Way through the Buddha's gate; why do you keep circling in the worlds of suffering so long? From beginningless time until now you have turned your back on awakening, gone along with afflictions and fallen into delusion. Always doing every kind of harm, you entered the three painful paths; not cultivating good, you sank into the karmic sea of the four kinds of birth. Because the body followed the six thieves, falling into evil realms was bitter beyond measure; because the mind turned from the One Vehicle, even when born human you were born before or after a Buddha. Now you have fortunately gained a human body, but it is the latter age after the Buddha's passing. Alas, whose fault is this?
j01.commentary: "Master within" calls to oneself, the true master inside. It is called Self-Admonitions because it rebukes and awakens oneself, not others. "The six thieves" likens the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind to thieves that chase objects and steal away one's merit.

j02.heading: Only People Change with the Times
j02.plain: Yet you turned yourself around, cut off attachment and left home; you took up the bowl, put on the Dharma robe, set foot on the shortcut out of the dusty world and learned the wondrous Dharma free of affliction. It is like a dragon finding water or a tiger taking to the mountains; its excellence cannot be fully told. People have past and present, but the Dharma is neither far nor near; people are foolish or wise, but the Way neither flourishes nor declines. Even in the Buddha's lifetime, what use is it if you do not follow the teaching? Even in the latter age, what harm is there if you uphold and practice it?
j02.commentary: This cuts off the excuse that awakening is hard in a degenerate age. The teaching does not grow old with the times; the problem is not the era but practice.

j03.heading: A Good Doctor and a Good Guide
j03.plain: So the World-Honored One said: "I am like a good doctor who knows the illness and prescribes the medicine; whether it is taken or not is not the doctor's fault. I am also like a good guide who leads people on a good road; if they hear and do not go, it is not the guide's fault. I have provided everything in the Dharma that benefits self and others; even if I stayed long, there would be no more benefit. From now on, if my disciples carry it on and practice it, the Tathāgata's Dharma body will always remain and never perish." If you understand this, you will only lament that you do not cultivate the Way yourself; why worry about the latter age? I hope you will set a firm resolve and open a broad mind, let go of all ties and remove upside-down thinking. Truly for the great matter of birth and death, contemplate well the gong'an of the patriarchs, aim at great awakening, and never belittle yourself and turn back.
j03.commentary: This quotes the Buddha's last teaching from the Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching. The medicine has already been given; taking it is up to us. That image is the spirit of the whole text. Next come the ten practices.

j04.heading: First, Do Not Accept Fine Clothes and Rich Food
j04.plain: First, never accept soft clothes and delicious food. From plowing and sowing until it reaches the mouth and body, not only is the labor of people and oxen great, but the harm to other lives is endless. It is not right to make others toil for my benefit; how much less can I bear to kill others to keep myself alive? Farmers always suffer hunger and cold, and weavers have no clothes to cover themselves; how then can I, sitting idle, resent hunger and cold? Soft clothes and fine food only add to the debt of kindness and diminish the Way; worn clothes and plain vegetables lighten the donor's burden and accumulate merit. If you do not illuminate the mind in this life, even a drop of water is hard to digest. Verse: With vegetable roots and tree fruit I will ease my hunger; with pine needles and grass clothing I will cover my body; with cranes of the field and blue clouds as companions, I will spend my remaining years among high peaks and deep valleys.
j04.commentary: It makes us reflect that everything we eat and wear holds the labor and lives of countless others. The saying that offerings received without illuminating the mind are heavy even as a drop of water is sharp.

j05.heading: Second, Do Not Hoard Your Own or Seek Others' Things
j05.plain: Second, do not cling to your own possessions and do not seek others' things. Among the sufferings of the three painful paths, the karma of greed comes first; among the six pāramitās, giving comes first. Stinginess and greed block the good paths; compassionate giving surely blocks the evil paths. When the poor come begging, do not be stingy even if you are in want. We came with nothing and leave empty-handed. You should have no attachment even to your own things; why set your mind on others'? Nothing can be taken along; only karma follows the body. A mind cultivated for three days is a treasure for a thousand years; things coveted for a hundred years are dust in a single morning. Verse: What is the root from which the three painful paths arise? Only the greed and attachment of many lives. With the robe and bowl our Buddha gave, our livelihood is ample; why store things up and feed ignorance?
j05.commentary: "Empty-handed we come, empty-handed we go" and "a mind cultivated for three days is a treasure for a thousand years; things coveted for a hundred years are dust in a morning" are well-known lines. Giving is urged as the way to cut off greed.

j06.heading: Third, Do Not Talk Much or Move Lightly
j06.plain: Third, do not talk much and do not move the body lightly. If the body does not move lightly, agitation stills and meditation is achieved; if the mouth does not talk much, delusion turns and wisdom is achieved. True reality is beyond words; true principle is not movement. The mouth is the gate of disaster, so guard it strictly; the body is the root of calamity, so do not move it lightly. A bird that flies often meets the sudden disaster of the net; a beast that roams lightly does not escape the harm of the arrow. So the World-Honored One sat unmoving for six years in the Snowy Mountains, and Bodhidharma stayed silent for nine years at Shaolin. How can later practitioners of Seon not follow these old footsteps? Verse: Holding body and mind, there is originally no movement; sitting silent in a thatched hut, I cut off coming and going. Still and silent, with not a single affair, I will just see the mind-Buddha and take refuge in myself.
j06.commentary: This teaches that speaking and acting less is itself the way to meditation and wisdom, citing the Buddha's practice in the Snowy Mountains and Bodhidharma's nine years facing the wall as examples.

j07.heading: Fourth, Keep Only Good Friends, Not Bad Ones
j07.plain: Fourth, stay close only to good friends and do not associate with bad ones. When a bird wants to rest it always chooses its forest; when a person wants to learn they choose teachers and friends. Choose the forest well and your rest is peaceful; choose teachers and friends well and your learning rises. So serve good friends as you would your parents, and keep away from bad friends as from enemies. The crane has no wish to befriend crows; how could the great roc make plans with a wren? A vine wrapped around a pine climbs straight up a thousand feet; a tree among cogon grass never grows past three feet. Often leave the company of the unkind, and often draw near to those of high attainment. Verse: Whether staying or walking, be with good friends; guard body and mind and clear away the thorny thickets of affliction. Sweep away the thickets entirely and the road ahead opens; without moving a step, you will break through the patriarchs' barrier.
j07.commentary: The Buddha said that good friendship is the whole of the holy life. Like the vine that climbs the pine, who we are with changes us.

j08.heading: Fifth, Sleep Only in the Middle of the Night
j08.plain: Fifth, allow yourself sleep only in the middle of the night. Of all that has blocked the Way for long ages, nothing is greater than the demon of sleep. Through all twelve hours of the day keep the questioning clear and undimmed, and while walking, standing, sitting and lying down, turn the light back and examine yourself without a gap. Waste a lifetime and you will lament for ten thousand kalpas. Impermanence comes in an instant, so be startled and afraid each day; human life is brief and truly cannot be guaranteed from moment to moment. If you have not broken through the patriarchs' barrier, how can you sleep at ease? Verse: Covered by the snake and clouds of sleep, the mind-moon is dark; practitioners who reach this point all lose their way. If here you take up the sword so sharp it cuts a hair blown against it, the clouds will vanish without a trace and the moon will shine of itself.
j08.commentary: The middle of the night here is roughly 11 p.m. to 1 a.m. Sparing sleep and staying awake can be read not as overworking the body but as a plea to stay clearly aware at all times.

j09.heading: Sixth, Do Not Exalt Yourself or Look Down on Others
j09.plain: Sixth, never carelessly exalt yourself and look down on others. In cultivating kindness and righteousness, humility and yielding are the root; in making friends, respect comes first. Piling up the mountain of self only adds to the sea of the three painful paths. Though you show dignity outwardly and seem lofty, if you have gained nothing within you are like a rotten boat. The higher one's rank, the lower one's heart; the deeper one's virtue, the humbler one's intent. Where the mountain of self and others crumbles, the Way of non-doing is accomplished by itself; to those who lower their hearts, every blessing returns by itself. Verse: In the dust of pride the jewel of wisdom is buried; on the mountain of self and others ignorance grows. Slighting others and never learning, tottering into old age, lying sick and groaning, your regrets will have no end.
j09.commentary: Lowering the heart (haseim) is the virtue most often stressed in Korean Buddhist practice. The higher one rises, the lower the heart should become.

j10.heading: Seventh, Meet Wealth and Sex with Right Thought
j10.plain: Seventh, when you see wealth or the opposite sex, always meet them with right thought. Nothing harms the body more than sexual desire, and nothing causes the loss of the Way more than wealth. That is why the Buddha laid down precepts strictly forbidding them. When the eye sees the opposite sex, look as if at a tiger or a snake; when the body meets gold and jade, see them as wood or stone. Even in a dark room, act as if before an honored guest, the same hidden or seen, with no difference inside and out. When the mind is pure, good spirits surely protect you; when drawn by lust, heaven does not tolerate you. With the spirits' protection there is no difficulty even in difficult places; without heaven's tolerance there is no peace even in peaceful places. Verse: Profit and desire become King Yama leading you to hell; pure conduct becomes Amitābha welcoming you to the lotus seat. Bound in chains and entering hell, the suffering is a thousandfold; when the lotus blooms on the ship of prajñā, the joy is ten-thousandfold.
j10.commentary: Written for monastics, it is strict about attraction to the opposite sex. Today it can be read as a teaching not to lose awareness before anything that captures the mind.

j11.heading: Eighth, Do Not Mingle with the World and Earn Resentment
j11.plain: Eighth, do not mingle with the world and earn others' dislike and envy. One who has left attachment in the heart is called a śramaṇa; one who does not long for the world is said to have left home. Having already cut off attachment and left the world, why form crowds with lay people again? Longing for the world makes you a greedy beast, and greed is not originally the mind of the Way. When human ties are thick, the mind of the Way grows thin; let worldly feeling cool and never look back. If you do not want to betray the intent of leaving home, go into famous mountains and seek the wondrous meaning to the end. With one robe and one bowl, cut off worldly ties; with no mind for hunger or fullness, the Way rises by itself. Verse: Even small good deeds done for others or for oneself are all causes of birth and death in saṃsāra. I wish to enter where the pine wind blows and the moon hangs in the vines, and forever contemplate the patriarchs' Seon free of affliction.
j11.commentary: A warning that entanglement in worldly ties blurs the intent of practice. For lay practitioners, it can be read as guarding one's practice time without being pulled around by relationships.

j12.heading: Ninth, Do Not Speak of Others' Faults
j12.plain: Ninth, do not speak of others' faults. Whether you hear good words or bad, do not let your mind be moved. Being praised without virtue is truly my shame; being slandered for real faults is truly my joy. Rejoicing, one knows one's faults and surely corrects them; ashamed, one advances on the Way without laziness. Do not speak of others' faults; in the end it will surely harm you. When you hear words that harm others, take them as if your own parents were being slandered. If this morning you speak of others' faults, another day they will turn and speak of yours. Yet all that has form is illusory; what is there to fear in slander or rejoice in praise? Verse: Carelessly speaking of others' rights and wrongs all morning, and enjoying dull sleep all night: leaving home like this only wastes the donors' offerings, and it will be hard to escape the three realms.
j12.commentary: The paradox of being ashamed of praise and glad of slander is deep. At the end it cites the Diamond Sutra, "All that has form is illusory," telling us not to be swayed by either praise or blame.

j13.heading: Tenth, Keep an Even Mind in the Assembly
j13.plain: Tenth, when among the assembly, always keep your mind even. Cutting off attachment and leaving one's parents is in order to see the whole Dharma realm equally. If you discriminate between near and far, your mind is not even; though you have left home, what virtue is there? If the mind has no hating or liking, no grasping or rejecting, how could the body have pain or pleasure, rise or fall? In the nature of equality there is no you or me; on the great round mirror, near and far are cut off. Going in and out of the three painful paths comes from being tangled in hate and love; rising and falling through the six realms comes from being bound by the karma of discriminating near and far. When the mind accords with equality, there is originally nothing to grasp or reject; with no grasping or rejecting, where is birth and death? Verse: To accomplish the way of supreme awakening, always hold an even mind. If you count near and far, hated and liked, the Way grows farther and karma grows deeper.
j13.commentary: This shares the spirit of the Inscription on Faith in Mind: "The supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing." An even mind that lays down liking and disliking completes the ten practices.

j14.heading: Conclusion
j14.plain: Master within, being born human is like a blind turtle in the sea meeting a floating log. How long is one lifetime, that you would idle without practice? A human body is hard to gain, and the Buddha-Dharma is hard to meet. Miss this life and you will hardly meet them again in ten thousand kalpas. Be sure to keep the precepts of the ten gates, practice diligently, advance with courage, and never turn back.
j14.commentary: The image of a blind turtle that surfaces once in a hundred years and meets a log with a hole in it means that being born human and meeting the Dharma is just that rare.

six-thieves.definition: The six senses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, likened to thieves that chase objects and steal away the good mind.

gongan.definition: An exchange or phrase of the patriarchs that Seon practitioners contemplate to bring about awakening.

paramita.definition: The six practices of a bodhisattva: giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation and wisdom.

four-marks.definition: The four attachments named in the Diamond Sutra: the notion of a self, of a person, of a being and of a life.
